table.brief: Three-level column header (Region > Country > Q1/Q2) with a corner cell spanning 3 header rows

understanding.purpose: Compare 2024 quarterly solar PV capacity additions across four country markets and three market segments, including totals, to judge scale, quarter-on-quarter movement, and country/segment mix.
understanding.reading: Readers scan down the segment rows, then compare Q1 vs Q2 within each country and compare country blocks across Europe and Asia-Pacific; the totals row anchors overall scale. The header hierarchy is region → country → quarter.
groups: Column 1 is the row-key/segment axis and must read as one unit.
Columns 2–5 form the Europe block: Germany Q1/Q2 followed by France Q1/Q2; each adjacent quarter pair belongs together, and the two countries are directly comparable.
Columns 6–9 form the Asia-Pacific block: Japan Q1/Q2 followed by Australia Q1/Q2, using the same country-then-quarter logic.
keep_intact: all numeric values, especially thousands-separated figures such as 2,330 and 2,065
country names in the merged header spans
row labels ideally, especially “Commercial & industrial” and “Residential rooftop”
may_wrap: country and region header text within its merged span
but not numeric cells; splitting 820 or 2,330 destroys comparison

preferred.name: r1A
preferred.note: Equalize every quarter column to 61px, the widest minimum needed by 2,065/2,330. This removes all pair and country-span jitter: Germany/France/Japan/Australia spans become 122px each and Europe/Asia 244px each. Keeps every number and Q1/Q2 intact; accepts 236px horizontal scroll rather than splitting data.

preferred.name: r3A
preferred.note: Set all eight quarter columns to the true 61px minimum (40px content for 2,330/2,065 plus 1px slack) and keep col 1 at 107px so "Segment" and "Commercial" stay whole. This is the tightest layout that keeps every figure and word intact — 595px total instead of 604–612 — cutting overflow to the irreducible ~235px while preserving exact symmetry between quarters, countries and the two region blocks. Horizontal scroll is unavoidable here (the table cannot fit 360px without splitting numbers, which would destroy the Q1-vs-Q2 comparison), so the right move is to accept the scroll at its minimum and keep the grid perfectly regular.

acceptable.name: r1B
acceptable.note: Equalize all non-German quarter columns to 59px, keeping Germany at 61px for its four-digit totals. Country pairs now match at 118px (Germany 122px), and the table is 12px narrower than uniform-61 while still avoiding all mid-word splits.

acceptable.name: r1C
acceptable.note: Minimal refinement of r0A: widen only Australia Q1 from 49px to 59px so its Q1/Q2 pair matches, leaving France Q1 at its 54px minimum. Saves 5px versus even-pairs and 17px versus uniform-61, but France remains a 54/59 pair, so the rhythm is less even.

acceptable.name: r2A
acceptable.note: Give every quarter column one uniform 63px width: 2px of slack over the 40px '2,330' so no figure can wrap, and identical rhythm for all four countries. Chosen specifically so col 1 (107) + Europe's four columns (4×63 = 252) = 359px — exactly the frame — meaning the visible box ends on the Europe/Asia-Pacific block boundary instead of slicing Japan Q1 in half. Scroll remains (252px) but the frame now shows a complete, untruncated logical block rather than orphaned digits.

acceptable.name: r2B
acceptable.note: Minimal uniform width that still clears the widest number with 1px slack, cutting the total to 603px — the least scroll achievable while keeping all eight quarter columns identical and every figure unsplit. Trades the clean block boundary for a 5px sliver of Japan Q1 at the frame edge; worth considering if horizontal scrolling is the primary constraint rather than the first-screen impression.

acceptable.name: r2C
acceptable.note: Keep Europe at 63px (preserves the exact 359px Europe-in-frame fit and slack for 2,330) but trim Asia-Pacific to 61px, which is still safe because its widest total is 1,64x (38px). Each region stays internally uniform and each Q1/Q2 pair stays equal, so comparison within a country is undistorted; the only cost is an 8px scroll reduction and a 2px width step at the region boundary.

bad.name: r3B
bad.note: An unexplored alternative: since the reader scrolls horizontally regardless, spend the extra width on the row axis instead of shaving it. At 195px col 1 carries 174px of content, so "Residential rooftop", "Commercial & industrial", "Utility-scale" and "Community solar" all sit on one line and every row collapses from 60px to 36px. The table becomes roughly 100px shorter, the row labels stop competing with the data for attention, and each row reads as a single horizontal unit — a better scan for a table whose job is comparing rows across many narrow columns. Cost: 683px total, about 88px more scroll than uniform-min, traded for a visibly calmer, shorter body.
bad.why: The 195px Segment column takes over half of the 360px viewport, so only Germany's Q1/Q2 are fully visible and France is cut off. It makes every row one line, but at 684px total width and 324px overflow it sacrifices the country/quarter comparison that is the table's main job.

rationale: This is a hierarchical comparison table: Segment rows, country groups, then Q1/Q2 leaves. At 360px it cannot fit, so the design should minimize horizontal travel while keeping every quarter column equal and every number/header intact. r1A/r3A do that with 61px leaf columns and a 107px Segment column that wraps labels only at spaces or hyphens; their first viewport still contains all of Europe. r1C saves 17px but makes France Q1 narrower than Q2, breaking the pair rhythm, while r3B over-invests in the Segment column and hides most of the numeric comparison.

general: Sibling leaf columns such as quarters should be equal width so Q1/Q2 pairs scan as units; parent groups should be built from those equal leaves.
When a table must overflow a narrow viewport, spend width on the columns that support comparison, not on forcing row labels onto one line.
Wrap multi-word row labels at spaces or hyphens rather than widening the identifier column until it dominates the table.
Numeric columns can be sized to the longest unbreakable token plus padding, not to the full one-line label width.
specific: The quarter columns need about 61px (40px content plus 21px padding) to keep 4-digit comma numbers and Q1/Q2 headers intact.
The Segment column needs 107px to keep 'Residential' and 'Commercial' unbroken; 195px makes all labels one line but pushes Europe out of the first viewport.
All candidates overflow 360px; r1A/r3A are the narrowest designs that keep every quarter column equal and every cell on one line.
The country groups are two-column pairs; r1C's 54px France Q1 breaks that pair even though it avoids a word split.

tradeoffs: A designer could reasonably prefer r3B's one-line rows and shorter 291px height over r1A's 384px height, accepting more horizontal scrolling. Conversely, r1C's 17px narrower table may be worth a slightly uneven France Q1 column. The equal-width 61px quarter columns are a rhythm choice, not a hard content minimum; col4 could shrink to 54px and col8 to 49px without splitting their own content.
uncertain: Whether row-label wrapping is acceptable in a horizontally scrolling table, and whether the first column would be sticky in the real implementation. The exact tolerance for column width is also uncertain because individual label widths were not provided; the ranges assume no change in line count or word integrity.

critique.good: Closest to a usable no-split layout: the 107px segment column wraps only at spaces, every numeric cell and Q1/Q2 label stays intact, and the region→country→quarter hierarchy is clear.
critique.problems: Still overflows the phone box by 209px. The data columns are visibly uneven: France Q1 is 54px vs Q2 59px, and Australia Q1 is 49px vs Q2 59px, so paired quarters do not align. Merged country spans are 122/113/118/108px, giving a jittery rhythm across the grid.
critique.cause: Widths were set to each column's individual minimum—driven by 1,115 in France Q1 and the smaller Australia Q1 values—rather than to a common quarter width. No width was spent on pair parity.

critique.good: Comfortable numeric cells with no splits, clear header hierarchy, and Europe is easy to read. Row labels wrap only at word boundaries.
critique.problems: Widest design, overflowing by 268px, so even less of Asia-Pacific is visible. Column 1 is 130px, yet “Residential rooftop” and “Commercial & industrial” still wrap, so the extra width buys no row-label benefit. Data columns are uneven at 70/61/63/59/68/59/58/59px, making Q1/Q2 pairs and country spans irregular.
critique.cause: Extra width was put into column 1 without reaching the roughly 193px needed for one-line row labels, while data columns received arbitrary minimum-plus-padding widths. This increases horizontal scroll without improving structure.

critique.good: Only 52px overflow, and the full region/country header structure is nearly visible. Row labels still break at word boundaries.
critique.problems: Every data column is 38px, leaving only 17px for text, so numbers split into digit stacks: 820 becomes 8/2/0, 2,330 becomes 2,/0/3/5/0, Q1/Q2 become Q/1 and Q/2, and “Germany” becomes “Germa/ny.” Rows become 3–6 lines, the table grows to 570px tall, and comparison is destroyed—yet it still overflows.
critique.cause: Forcing the total near 360px by making all quarter columns 38px ignores the 49–61px minimum needed for the numeric content. The narrow width was applied uniformly instead of respecting content minima.

critique.good: The only fully honest allocation: 107px for col 1 keeps 'Residential' and 'Commercial' whole, and eight identical 61px quarter columns give the Q1/Q2 pairs perfect symmetry, keep every figure (including 2,330) on one line, and let the merged Europe › Germany/France header stack read cleanly. Europe is completely visible inside the frame, so the within-Europe comparison the table is built for works.
critique.problems: The table is 596px wide against a 360px frame, so the entire Asia-Pacific half — Japan and Australia, all eight of their values and both country totals — is off-screen; the reader cannot make the Europe-vs-Asia-Pacific comparison that is the table's stated purpose. The frame edge also slices through Japan Q1, leaving orphaned '63…', '41…', '52…', '80…' fragments that look like broken data rather than an invitation to scroll.
critique.cause: Structural, not tuning: col 1 cannot go below 107px without splitting 'Residential' (86px + 21px padding), and no quarter column can go below 61px without splitting '2,330' (40px + 21px). 107 + 8×61 = 595 is the absolute floor, so ~236px of overflow is unavoidable; no width choice can remove it.

critique.good: Preserves Q1/Q2 pair equality and keeps every number intact; the six 59px columns still clear '1,232' (38px), so nothing wraps. Total is trimmed slightly.
critique.problems: Germany's pair (61/61) is now visibly wider than France's (59/59), producing a subtly ragged rhythm with no content justification — the widest German total (2,330, 40px) and the widest French total (1,232, 38px) differ by 2px, and both columns sit at zero slack, so the narrowing buys nothing visible. Asia-Pacific is still entirely outside the frame and the Japan column is still sliced.
critique.cause: Shaving 2px off six columns: a 12px saving against a 224px overflow, i.e. invisible, while the unequal country pairs do register to the eye.

critique.good: Correctly identifies col 4 (France Q1, 33px of content) as the one column with genuine slack and tries to reclaim it.
critique.problems: It breaks the Q1/Q2 symmetry inside France: France Q1 is narrower than France Q2 although they hold identically formatted numbers meant to be read as a pair, so the narrow cell reads as subordinate. At 54px the content is exactly 33px, zero slack, so '410' and '1,115' are one font-metric change away from wrapping. And it still overflows by 219px with Asia-Pacific invisible.
critique.cause: 5px reclaimed from a column whose pair partner stays at 59, at the cost of pair symmetry and wrap safety; the overflow is unaffected because it is driven by col 1 + 8 quarter columns, not by this one cell.

critique.good: The strongest of the three. All eight quarter columns are identical at 63px (42px of content against a 40px need), so every Q1/Q2 pair is equal, each country's two columns are equal, and the merged Germany/France/Japan/Australia spans sit perfectly centred over their pairs. No number splits, the three-tier header (region → country → quarter) reads cleanly, and rows are stable at 60px.
critique.problems: Column 1 is set to exactly 107px, which is 86px of content against a 86px longest word — zero slack, so the "Segment" header sits flush to the padding edge and looks pinched next to the generous data columns. The table also measures 612px, i.e. 17px more overflow than the content actually requires, buying no visible improvement.
critique.cause: Uniform 63px data columns (42px content where 40px suffices) plus a row-header column sized to the exact glyph width of "Segment".

critique.good: Tightest of the three at 604px while still keeping every figure whole; the even 62px rhythm preserves the quarter-pair and country-pair symmetry and the merged header spans remain centred. Good economy without any visual cost.
critique.problems: 62px leaves 41px of content for a 40px widest value ("2,330", "2,065") — a single pixel of slack. Any rounding, font fallback or slightly wider comma pushes those cells into a mid-number split, which is precisely the failure this table cannot afford. Column 1 still has no slack.
critique.cause: Columns shaved to 62px, landing the widest numeric cell within 1px of breaking.

critique.good: Attempts to differentiate the two region blocks and keeps all numbers intact; nothing splits and row heights stay even.
critique.problems: The 63/61 split between the Europe block and the Asia-Pacific block is arbitrary and visually legible as an inconsistency: the Japan and Australia columns are narrower than Germany and France even though their content is narrower, not wider. The reader comparing across regions now sees two blocks with different rhythm and a misaligned seam at the region boundary, which undercuts the very comparison the table exists to support.
critique.cause: Last four columns set to 61px while the first four stay at 63px, with no content reason.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

r3B.why: The first column is far wider than needed; row labels stay on one line, but only Germany Q1/Q2 and France Q1 fit, cutting the France group and hiding Asia. Readable, but it wastes width and blocks comparison.

r1C.why: Row labels wrap at word boundaries, all Germany/France quarters stay intact, Japan Q1 begins in view, and numbers remain unbroken. A sensible 360px compromise.

r1A.why: All Europe columns are readable and words/numbers stay intact, but the viewport cuts through Japan’s Q1 header and value, making the right edge look accidental.

r1B.why: Similar to C: clean Europe view and intact numbers, but the first Asia column is sliced mid-header and mid-value at the viewport edge.

ref_equal.why: Columns are squeezed so every label, header and number breaks vertically into letters and digits; the table is unreadable as a table.

ref_auto.why: Like B: compact first column with clean word wrapping, complete Germany/France quarter groups, intact numbers, and Japan Q1 visible at the edge.

raw.unsure: B and F look nearly identical at this scale; exact width differences among B–F are subtle, and C/D might be slightly more comfortable for numbers despite cutting Japan Q1.

r1C.why: Column 1 is wide enough for the longest word (Residential/Commercial stay whole, labels wrap cleanly to two lines), and every numeric column holds its Q1/Q2 header and values like 2,065 on one line. Group headers Europe/Germany/France stay legible, row rhythm is even. Only cost is horizontal scroll, which is unavoidable here.

ref_auto.why: Essentially the same as A: a ~110px Segment column with tidy two-line wraps and intact numbers/quarter headers. Indistinguishable from A at this scale; nothing is split or clipped inside a column.

r3B.why: Widening Segment to ~195px lets 'Commercial & industrial' sit on one line, which helps row identification, but it eats roughly 1.5 numeric columns of the 360px viewport (only Germany Q1/Q2 and part of France Q1 visible), so cross-country comparison needs much more scrolling for a modest gain; numbers themselves stay intact.

r1B.why: Same clean wrapping of row labels as A with slightly wider numeric columns (~63–65px), so values and Q1/Q2 headers are comfortably intact and well spaced. Total width is a touch larger, but the visible comparison set is the same and readability is good.

ref_equal.why: Squeezed to the 360px box: every word and number is broken letter by letter ('S e g m e n t', 'R e s i d e n t i a l', '8 2 0', '1, 5 5'), destroying words, numbers and row identity. Unreadable as a table.

r1A.why: Close to A: Segment column wide enough to keep 'Residential'/'Commercial' whole with two-line wraps, numeric columns intact with clear Q1/Q2 headers. Only minor clipping at the viewport edge, not within columns.

raw.unsure: A, B, D and F render almost identically at this resolution (differences of 1–3px in column 1 vs numeric widths), so ranking among them is near-arbitrary; C's one-line row labels are a defensible trade-off if a frozen first column were assumed; and I cannot verify whether horizontal scrolling is penalised by the evaluation, which would change how C is judged.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
